items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [climatechangenews.com] COP17 urges subsidy cuts as nature finance gap persists before COP31
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Governments at the U.N. biodiversity summit, COP17, agreed to accelerate efforts to cut subsidies that damage nature, including support for fossil fuels, but left unresolved how to fund conservation. Nearly 200 countries adopted the Yerevan Pathway in Armenia after the first review found the world off track on almost all biodiversity goals for 2030. The agreement calls for countries to revise their biodiversity plans to address gaps in marine, coastal and inland-water protection and accelerate efforts to reduce harmful incentives by at least $500 billion a year by 2030. Developed countries missed a commitment to provide at least $20 billion annually for nature by 2025, while environmental funding is projected to fall 27% over 2026-30, Carbon Brief reported. Organizers said governments, philanthropies and investors announced more than $1.8 billion in nature finance at the summit, compared with the framework’s goal of mobilizing $200 billion a year by 2030. Countries invited non-donor states to express interest in joining the donor list, but deferred a decision on the structure of a permanent post-2030 financing mechanism until COP18 in Quito in 2028. The U.N. climate conference COP31 begins in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 9.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Oklahoma will prohibit data centers from using groundwater for evaporative cooling starting Nov. 1, requiring closed-loop or immersion systems under a new law. The restriction applies to water use inside facilities, but electricity generation can account for a larger share of data centers’ water footprint. The law follows drought conditions in western Oklahoma during much of 2026; Pennsylvania has separately required data centers using more than 10 megawatts to disclose energy and water use. Forbes cited national figures showing that power plants serving data centers consumed far more water in 2023 than data centers used for cooling.

items.title: [pbs.org] Super El Niño nears December peak as extreme weather spreads
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The exceptionally strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is intensifying weather risks across several regions, including heavy rain and flash floods in the U.S. Southwest. Scientists say the pattern adds moisture to the air and shifts winds, making downpours more likely, although it is not the sole cause of individual storms. The World Meteorological Organization expects the event to peak in December and persist into February 2027. The agency says it could rank among the strongest since at least 1950. Flooding has also been reported in Peru and Ecuador, while Indonesia and parts of Southeast Asia are unusually dry. In the Southwest, flooding prompted evacuations, and the San Juan River threatened Pagosa Springs, Colorado. Warmer oceans linked to human-caused climate change may amplify the event’s effects, but scientists caution that separating El Niño’s contribution from the long-term warming trend remains difficult. In September, sea-surface temperature in the Pacific’s Niño 3.4 reference region reached 29.70°C, while the global ocean average for that month, excluding polar waters, set a September record of 21.05°C. Forecasters expect the strongest effects to continue into 2027.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A seven-year field experiment on King George Island found that Antarctica’s only two native flowering plants responded in opposite ways to warming: Antarctic hair grass showed reduced water flow through its leaves and lower photosynthesis, while Antarctic pearlwort showed increases in both. The findings come from plants grown in open-top chambers near Poland’s Henryk Arctowski Antarctic Station. The chambers produced sharp temperature swings, not just higher average temperatures: during the 2018–19 summer, plants inside spent far more time below freezing than those outside. Researchers are now examining plants that have remained in the chambers for 16 years, along with microorganisms living around them.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says the strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and is nearly certain to persist until February 2027. The climate pattern, which warms the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is forecast to bring above-average temperatures across much of the world and shift rainfall patterns, increasing drought and flood risks in different regions. In Ecuador, the Navy’s Oceanographic and Antarctic Institute reported sea temperatures as much as 5.2°C above normal off Ecuador and Peru. It linked the unusually warm water to exceptional coastal rainfall, rainfall deficits in the Andean highlands and Amazon, and reduced nutrient levels affecting some fisheries. Officials urged preparations for coastal flooding. Separately, Copernicus reported that the global average sea-surface temperature outside polar regions reached a September record of 21.05°C.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Sweden’s valuable meadows and grazing lands have largely retained their natural and cultural value, according to an analysis by the Swedish Board of Agriculture. Of 300,000 hectares identified as valuable, 260,000 had been fully inventoried. In 2020, nearly 70% of that fully inventoried area — 175,000 hectares — received environmental management payments, 8,000 hectares more than in 2018. Repeat surveys conducted 10 to 20 years apart found that most inventoried sites remained meadows or pastures. Some sites lost value when left unmanaged and became overgrown, while restoration helped recover value elsewhere. The agency says continued inventories are needed to track changes.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

items.title: [insideclimatenews.org] China powers AI data centers with renewables as U.S. gas expansion looms
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

China is pairing its expanding artificial-intelligence data center sector with renewable power, while U.S. developers are increasingly turning to gas-fired generation. Envision Energy began operating a renewable-powered data center campus in Inner Mongolia in August and says it plans to expand the site beyond 2 gigawatts. China’s policy targets renewable sources for more than 80% of the electricity used by new data centers in major computing hubs. In the United States, Wood Mackenzie projects annual additions of 13.2 to 16.4 gigawatts of gas-fired capacity from 2026 through 2035, more than three times the 2023-25 annual average. A Sierra Club analysis cited by Inside Climate News estimates emissions from new off-grid data centers could reach levels comparable to Mexico’s annual emissions by 2030. Geothermal developer Fervo Energy’s chief executive said grid connection delays and a difficult financing market are weighing on the sector.

Intruders accessed connected refrigeration controllers and changed equipment settings in cyberattacks on supermarkets across Europe on Nov. 2. Some affected systems used equipment from Danish manufacturer Danfoss, whose equipment was also targeted in France in October. Authorities have not established who was responsible or whether the incidents were linked. Security reports point to management interfaces intended for closed networks but exposed to the internet, as well as older controllers that no longer receive security updates. Stephan Moelans, chief executive of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, said some affected units need physical modifications as well as software changes to address the vulnerability. On Nov. 2, Italy’s National Cybersecurity Agency urged retailers, food logistics operators and refrigeration companies to strengthen security after attacks affected at least four Coop supermarkets in Sicily. Italian postal police were investigating, and a government security meeting was scheduled for Nov. 3. Authorities have not attributed the European incidents to anyone; Katrien Eggers, spokesperson for Belgium’s Centre for Cybersecurity, said the perpetrator may never be identified.

items.title: [phys.org] Researchers document sustained sexual bond between Ethiopian bull and male donkey
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

An Italian-led research team documented repeated sexual interactions between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau, describing a selective social bond between the animals. During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology. The pair also licked, rubbed and nuzzled one another, and researchers repeatedly saw them seek each other out despite access to other potential mates. The team cautions that observations of one domesticated pair cannot establish why the behavior occurred or what the animals felt. Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

items.title: [ncsc.gov.uk] UK cyber agency warns AI-powered ransomware could hit critical infrastructure by 2028
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the government’s cyber defense agency, said Tuesday that an AI-powered ransomware attack on Britain’s critical infrastructure is highly likely by 2028. Chief Executive Richard Horne warned that artificial intelligence is expected to help hostile actors find and exploit long-standing weaknesses faster and on a greater scale, rather than develop entirely new attack methods. Energy, transport, health and food systems are among the essential services at risk. The NCSC also warned of a likely rise in cyber incidents in the coming months, citing underinvestment, outdated systems and known vulnerabilities that organizations have not patched. It assessed China as the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK and said Russia and China are likely to use AI routinely for geopolitical aims by 2028. It also described Russian attempts to breach British military networks and Iranian cyber operations targeting the UK. The government has announced £60 million for the first phase of a national Cyber Shield and £70 million for a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre to help identify weaknesses across critical infrastructure and the economy. In its annual report, the NCSC is urging organizations to invest in resilience and basic protections.

items.title: [nasa.gov] 4.1-billion-year-old Mars meteorite reveals evidence of ancient water
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA-funded researchers say Teghaza 001, a meteorite found in Mali’s Sahara in 2022, formed in Mars’ crust at least 4.1 billion years ago, potentially making it the oldest of about 435 Martian meteorites identified on Earth. The study, published in Science on Oct. 29, describes a rare sample from the planet’s early crust; only three known Martian meteorites date to that period. The rock is a coarse-grained igneous material called gabbro, formed as magma cooled underground. Its oxygen and hydrogen isotope signatures, along with altered minerals, indicate that water reached deep into the crust and interacted with rock more than 4.1 billion years ago; the rock itself likely formed earlier. Spacecraft observations have also shown evidence of ancient water on Mars. Researchers say the evidence supports the possibility that early Mars had habitable conditions, but does not show that life existed there. Orbital mineral data point to 13 possible source locations in the planet’s southern highlands, but the meteorite’s precise birthplace remains unknown.
